newsitem.title: UK: Britons vote in election that could end an era.
newsitem.headline: Britons vote in election that could end an era.

text.p: Britons vote on Thursday in a landmark election expected to end an era that began 18 years ago when "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher became prime minister.
Opinion polls show the opposition Labour Party, led by moderniser Tony Blair, should win a landslide.

But neither Blair nor his rival, Prime Minister John Major, have given them much credence. The polls also show up to half of Britain's 44 million voters have not yet made up their minds, so much could still be at stake.
"It's not over till it's over" Blair has repeatedly said throughout the six-week campaign, the longest for over 80 years.
"I have not contemplated anything other than winning. I have a very positive attitude to this campaign," Major said late on Wednesday in one of the last interviews of his campaign.
At the same time, Blair was making last minute appeals to his supporters not to be complacent about a Labour victory.

"Twenty-four hours to go. Twenty-four hours in which the decision about the future of this country will be made," he said in a former mining village in north-east England where he began his career 14 years ago.

Opinion polls in Thursday's newspapers gave Labour leads of between 10 points and 22 points over the Conservatives. The 10 point lead in an ICM poll for the Guardian newspaper was the second lowest Labour has recorded during the campaign.

Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing from the 1992 election to win a majority in the 659-seat parliament and the latest polls suggest it could gain as much as a 15 percent swing, giving it a 200-seat majority.
But Labour has consistently said its own surveys suggest a much narrower gap between the two main parties.
The party has reason to be wary. It suffered a stunning defeat in the 1992 election, when opinion polls had shown it almost certain of victory.

Since then, Blair has transformed the party, shifting it to the centre ground of politics and winning over business leaders who would never have considered supporting the old Labour Party with its strong links to the unions and reputation for high taxes and profligacy.
His shadow finance minister Gordon Brown has pledged not to raise personal taxes for the life of the next parliament and has vowed to keep tight control on public spending.
With little left in policy differences between Labour and the Conservatives, a Labour victory will rely heavily on a feeling in Britain that it is time for a change.

Major's Conservatives, who stand to win an unprecedented fifth term of office if elected, have fought hard against this attitude, arguing that they are the only party with the experience to run Britain. Their campaign posters read "Britain Is Booming, Don't Let Labour Blow It."
But Major has spent most of his campaign on the back foot, battling the allegations of sleaze and the divisions over Europe that have dogged his party for most of the last five years.
He had hoped that his personal popularity -- polls consistently show he is better liked than his party is -- would win the day.
He said he arranged a long campaign in the hope that this would allow him to rally support for his party.
"I did deliberately seek a long campaign because I believed our opponents would obscure the issues in the first two weeks," he said.
But in the middle of the campaign, he was forced into an emergency broadcast, appealing to voters to disregard the views of the rebellious Euro-sceptics in his party.
And the final week of the election was the most bitter of all, with Major accusing Blair of telling "scurrilous lies" about the Conservatives' plans for state pensions.

If the Conservative do once more defy opinion polls and win Thursday's election, it will be the biggest political upset since 1945, when Britons ousted wartime prime minister Winston Churchill and elected Labour with a landslide.
